title: Athlete meal-prep briefs: portions, schedules and diet guidance
body_markdown:
Athlete meal prep is planned cooking around an athlete’s training schedule and agreed dietary guidance, with the aim of making suitable meals easier to organise. A useful athlete meal prep chef brief translates that guidance into portions, cooking dates, storage instructions and clear responsibilities. It tells the chef what to prepare without asking the chef to prescribe your diet.


**TL;DR**

- An athlete meal prep chef brief should separate dietary guidance from cooking instructions.
- myCHEF provides private chef meal prep; confirm the requirements of your athlete meal plan before booking.
- Specify portion measurements, training schedules, ingredient restrictions and storage arrangements before approving menus.
- Choose your cooking format around kitchen access and meal timing, not menu descriptions alone.


## Why a clear meal-prep brief matters for athletes

A training diary tells you when you exercise. It does not tell a chef which meals you need, whether ingredient weights refer to raw or cooked food, or which substitutions your dietary adviser accepts. Those details belong in the cooking brief.

For athletes, the practical challenge is keeping meals aligned with instructions when training, work and travel change. **The brief should make your requirements repeatable without turning the chef into your nutrition adviser.** Start with the distinction between a nutrition target and a kitchen instruction in this guide to [weekly meal prep around your macros](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/weekly-meal-prep-to-hitting-your-macros-complete-workflow).

myCHEF provides vetted chefs for home cooking and weekly meal preparation in Dubai. **myCHEF is best suited to athletes seeking private chef meal prep rather than a substitute for qualified dietary advice.** Confirm whether your particular portioning, ingredient and documentation requirements can be accommodated before agreeing the service.

## How to write an athlete meal prep chef brief

### Define who sets your dietary instructions

Start with a shared document. Put your current dietary instructions at the top, followed by the name or role of the person authorised to change them. If you work with a sports dietitian or another qualified clinician, ask for cooking-ready guidance rather than sending the chef fragments from several conversations.

Keep medical requirements separate from food preferences. An allergy, a prescribed restriction and a dislike of mushrooms require different handling; combining them under a single list of foods to avoid creates ambiguity.

A chef prepares food. Do not assume a private chef booking includes sports nutrition assessment, medical advice or interpretation of blood results. Ask which instructions the chef needs and take unresolved dietary questions back to the appropriate professional.

- Identify the owner of your dietary plan.
- Separate allergies, prescribed restrictions and preferences.
- Attach the current approved instructions, not superseded versions.
- State who approves substitutions or portion changes.
- Record any unresolved questions before menu approval.

### Map meals against your actual schedule

Use a calendar or spreadsheet before choosing dishes. Mark training, work, travel and the meals you already handle yourself. Your chef needs the eating occasions to cover, not simply a request for a week of healthy food.

Distinguish meals eaten at home from food carried to an office or training venue. Access to refrigeration, reheating equipment and somewhere to sit changes the practical menu. Do not assume a meal that works at your dining table works equally well in a changing room or between appointments.

For a hypothetical household of 2 adults ordering 6 lunches, specify that each person needs 3 lunches. That arithmetic establishes the cooking quantity; it says nothing about either person’s nutritional requirements. Assign each portion to a person and an eating occasion before requesting a quotation.

- List the meals the chef must prepare.
- Mark where each meal will be eaten.
- Record access to refrigeration and reheating.
- Flag travel dates and changing training times.
- Identify meals already covered elsewhere.

### Translate portions into kitchen instructions

Replace descriptions such as generous protein or light dinner with the measurements your dietary adviser has specified. State whether weights refer to ingredients before cooking or food after cooking. Water loss and absorption change food weight, so the two descriptions are not interchangeable.

Also distinguish a recipe total from an individual portion. A tray prepared for several people needs a clear allocation method if their instructions differ. Ask how the chef will measure, divide and identify portions; do not assume weighing or nutritional analysis forms part of every booking.

Once the document is clear, a myCHEF meal-prep enquiry can establish whether the cooking service fits it. The benefit is help with preparation; the limitation is that any requirement for precise nutrient calculations or specialist dietary supervision must be confirmed separately.

- Specify raw or cooked weights wherever measurements appear.
- Separate batch quantities from individual portions.
- Identify the intended recipient of each meal.
- Define whether sauces and dressings are included in measurements.
- Agree the information required on container labels.

### Agree menus and substitution rules

Build a short menu around foods you already tolerate and enjoy. Familiar meals make feedback more useful: you can identify an issue with texture, portioning or reheating without also judging an unfamiliar recipe.

An illustrative menu might include chicken with rice and vegetables, a lentil-based dish, and fish with potatoes. These are menu ideas, not a sports nutrition prescription. Your dietary instructions determine ingredients, quantities and suitability.

Substitutions deserve their own section. Replacing an ingredient changes more than the dish name, particularly where allergens or measured portions are involved. Specify which changes need approval and who gives it. Keep supplements outside routine recipe substitutions unless your qualified adviser has provided explicit instructions and the cooking arrangement supports them.

- List preferred dishes and ingredients you dislike.
- Attach approved recipes where exact preparation matters.
- Separate ingredient restrictions from cuisine preferences.
- State which substitutions require permission.
- Agree how menu changes will be recorded.

### Confirm the kitchen and service scope

Walk through your kitchen before requesting a cooking schedule. Check worktop space, hob and oven access, suitable pans, weighing equipment, containers and available refrigeration. A clear brief needs a workable place to cook and store the food.

For a Dubai apartment or villa, include building entry arrangements, parking instructions and who can admit the chef. Describe any shared kitchen use during the visit. These are planning details to agree, not assumed service inclusions.

Ask separately about shopping, ingredient payment, preparation, portioning, washing up and waste removal. A proposal should distinguish included work from tasks you retain. The guide to [how long a private chef home visit takes](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/how-long-does-a-private-chef-home-visit-take-in-dubai) covers the scheduling question to resolve alongside your menu.

- Describe kitchen equipment and usable storage space.
- Confirm access, parking and entry arrangements.
- Allocate responsibility for groceries and containers.
- Agree preparation, portioning and cleaning tasks.
- Identify anything excluded from the quotation.

### Set the handover and review process

Agree what happens after cooking, not just what appears on the menu. Request food-specific storage and reheating instructions, and establish who moves meals into storage. Do not assign every dish the same shelf life or assume a weekly cooking visit means every meal belongs in the fridge for the whole week.

Use a simple feedback log after the first agreed cooking session. Record whether portions matched the brief, meals reheated as intended and the schedule covered the right eating occasions. Send dietary changes to the person responsible for the plan rather than asking the chef to improvise.

Keep one current brief. A message changing a meal should also update the shared document, so the next cooking session does not rely on someone remembering an earlier conversation.

- Agree labels, storage instructions and reheating guidance.
- Assign responsibility for putting food away.
- Record practical feedback against individual dishes.
- Route dietary changes to the authorised adviser.
- Update the brief before the next session.

## Which meal-prep arrangement fits your routine?

**Choose the format that matches how you need food prepared and handed over.** Self-preparation gives you direct control but leaves the work with you. In-home cooking transfers preparation tasks but requires kitchen access. Prepared-meal delivery removes the home cooking visit, while the available menu and modification process need checking.

Dietetic support answers a different question: what your dietary plan should contain. It can sit alongside any cooking format rather than replace one.

| Option | Best for | Main advantage | Key limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Self-preparation | Athletes who want direct control over cooking | You manage ingredients, measurements and timing yourself | You retain shopping, cooking and washing up |
| In-home private chef | Athletes who want help preparing meals in their kitchen | Cooking can be planned around an agreed household brief | Kitchen access and the exact service scope need agreement |
| Prepared-meal delivery | Athletes who prefer meals prepared off-site | No cooking visit takes place in your home | Check available modifications, portion information and handover arrangements |
| Dietitian-led plan with separate cooking | Athletes who need individual dietary guidance translated into meals | Dietary decisions and cooking responsibilities remain distinct | Adviser and cook need a clear way to exchange approved instructions |


![Four arrangements for athlete meals: self-preparation, a private chef, delivery and a dietitian-led plan](https://gwvckixiegkllthleuyt.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/workspace-article-images-public/0dab3848-3d31-4eb1-875d-5c329ae6d865/body-b3c9289fa87f4a4035dcd8117387c1f6.jpg)

*Dietary guidance and meal preparation are separate responsibilities, even when they work together.*


## What should you compare in a proposal?

Compare the same brief across proposals. A quotation covering cooking alone is not directly comparable with one that also includes shopping, portioning and containers. Ask for the scope in writing before deciding.

Relevant price drivers include menu complexity, the number of distinct dishes, ingredient requirements, shopping responsibilities and the work requested during each visit. Do not use the number of containers as your only measure of workload: separate recipes and individually measured portions are different tasks from dividing a shared dish.

Clarify staffing and timing as well. Ask who will cook, whether anyone else is needed, and how the proposed visit fits your kitchen access. Vetted chefs are part of myCHEF’s stated service; specialist sports nutrition credentials and any particular reporting method require separate confirmation.

## Common mistakes athletes make in a chef brief

### Treating a training goal as a recipe

Requests such as fuel recovery or support race preparation do not specify what to cook. Provide the approved dietary instructions, then explain how meals must fit your routine. The chef should not have to infer portions from your sport.

### Mixing raw and cooked measurements

An ingredient weight without its measurement basis leaves room for inconsistent preparation. Mark the basis beside each instruction and use it consistently across recipes, portions and feedback.

### Ordering for an ideal week

A fixed menu built around a schedule you rarely follow creates avoidable gaps. Brief against your actual diary, including office days, late sessions and travel. Agree how changes are communicated before the next cooking visit.

### Leaving shared-household portions unlabelled

Food prepared for an athlete and other household members needs clear ownership when portions or ingredients differ. Identify recipients in the brief and agree a label format. Do not rely on container size alone.

### Assuming nutrition calculations are included

A measured portion is not automatically a verified nutrient calculation. Ask what information the cooking service provides, how it is produced and what your dietary adviser needs to review. Keep performance or medical decisions outside an unconfirmed service scope.

## FAQ


**What should an athlete meal prep chef brief include?**

An athlete meal prep chef brief should include approved dietary instructions, portion measurements, meal schedules, ingredient restrictions and kitchen arrangements. It should also identify who approves changes and how meals are labelled, stored and reheated.

**Can a private chef set my sports nutrition targets?**

Do not assume sports nutrition advice is included in a private chef service. Take individual dietary targets to an appropriately qualified professional and give the chef clear cooking instructions based on that guidance.

**Should I give a chef raw weights or cooked weights?**

Give the chef the measurement basis specified in your dietary instructions and label it explicitly. Raw and cooked weights are not interchangeable, so resolve any ambiguity before menu approval.

**Is an in-home chef better than meal delivery for an athlete?**

An in-home chef suits someone seeking cooking help in their own kitchen; delivery suits someone who does not want a home cooking visit. Compare each option against your portion requirements, menu restrictions and practical schedule rather than assuming either format guarantees a dietary match.

**Can the chef prepare different portions for my household?**

Request different household portions explicitly and confirm that the proposed service supports them. Identify each recipient, provide their instructions separately and agree how containers will be labelled.

**How do I compare quotations for athlete meal preparation?**

Compare quotations against the same written scope, including shopping, ingredients, cooking, portioning, containers and cleaning. Confirm exclusions and any specialist measurement or documentation requirements before accepting a proposal.

**What should I send with a meal-prep enquiry?**

Send your preferred start date, Dubai location, number of people and required cooking service. Add the eating occasions to cover, kitchen access details and any approved dietary instructions that affect preparation.

- [How long does meal prep stay fresh in the fridge?](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/how-long-does-meal-prep-stay-fresh-in-the-fridge)

## Start with the meal you find hardest to organise

Before requesting an entire menu, identify the eating occasion your current routine handles poorly. A brief centred on that practical gap is more useful than a long list of preferred dishes.

To discuss private chef meal preparation with myCHEF, send your preferred date, Dubai location, household headcount and service required. Include the meals you need covered and your approved dietary instructions so the cooking requirements can be assessed clearly.
